notes.shape: The yield curve plots Treasury yields across maturities from 1 month to 30 years, with a normal upward slope indicating higher yields for longer maturities due to time and risk premiums. An inverted curve, where short-term yields exceed long-term yields, historically signals economic downturns and recessions within 6 to 18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.71%, and the 10-year minus 2-year (2s10s) spread is 0.36 points, indicating an upward sloping curve. This represents a re-steepening from the deepest inversion at 0.0 points, after being inverted during 2022-2024.
notes.signal: The 2s10s spread acts as a key recession indicator, with inversion (spread below zero) having preceded every modern U.S. recession. The curve was inverted through 2022-2024 but has since moved above zero, signaling a re-steepening. However, the yield curve often un-inverts shortly before recessions actually begin, so an un-inverted curve does not rule out an upcoming downturn. The NY Fed assigns a 31% probability of recession, reflecting moderate risk consistent with the recent inversion and partial normalization of the curve.
notes.now: Currently, the yield curve’s modest positive slope and the 31% recession probability from the NY Fed suggest elevated economic uncertainty. The prior inversion’s unwinding indicates some easing of immediate recession risk, but the relatively low 2s10s spread and moderate recession probability reflect ongoing caution in the market about economic conditions.
